Thursday evening. Ioana and Julien go up to Madame Bernard’s. They have Hélène’s score in their hands. They don’t know how to begin.
Madame Bernard, we have something to show you. It’s a little delicate.
Come in, come in. Would you like some tea?
Yes, I’d love some, thank you.
This score was in our piano. Do you recognise the handwriting?
(A long silence.) But… it’s Henri’s handwriting. I recognise it straight away.
It was for a certain Hélène. We met her on Saturday. She’s eighty-three.
Hélène… Henri talked to me about her only once, before our wedding. He was crying when he told me.
That in Algeria he had been wounded in his left hand. He couldn’t play the piano any more. So he didn’t go back to Lyon. He was ashamed.
And he never wrote to her?
He did. But he never sent the letter. I kept it. It’s in this box, with the others.
Are you going to give it to her?
Yes. I’ll give it to her myself. Will you invite her to your party on Saturday?
Of course. Her nephew will bring her. And I’ll play the waltz.
One last thing. Every year, on 3 May, Henri used to whistle a waltz. Always the same one. I never knew why.
3 May? We’ll ask her on Saturday.
You know, you understand some things much better at seventy-five than at twenty. Come, I’ll show you his letters.

Three small syllables, linked: “zhuh-tuhl-don”. The e’s in te and le almost disappear in fast speech.
“Ee-lee-ã-na”, all linked, like a single word. Negative: “il n’y en a pas” = “ee-nya-na-pa”.
“Don-luh-mwa”: the stress falls on the last pronoun, “moi”.
“See-flay”: the double f is read as one, -ait = an open “e”.
Sometimes a sentence has both a direct and an indirect object: “Ioana gives the letter to Madame Bernard” → “Ioana gives it to her”. French puts both before the verb, in a fixed order:
He gives me the key. → He gives it to me.
I tell Hélène the truth. → I tell it to her.
Are you sending the photos to your parents? → Are you sending them to them?
There are croissants. → There are some.
Memory trick: “me/te/nous/vous” come BEFORE “le/la/les” (me le), but “lui/leur” come AFTER (le lui). Y and en always come last, and “en” is the very last of all.
2. In the past, the future and the negative
The pronoun group goes before the auxiliary (passé composé) or the conjugated verb (future). The negation goes around it:
I’m going to give it to her.
Il ne me l’a jamais dit.
In the passé composé, the past participle agrees with a direct object placed before it: “La lettre ? Je l’ai gardée.” (feminine → gardée). “Les photos ? Je les lui ai montrées.”
In the affirmative imperative, the pronouns move AFTER the verb, joined with hyphens, and the direct object comes first. “Me” and “te” become “moi” and “toi”:
In the NEGATIVE imperative the order goes back to normal: “Ne me le donne pas !” (Don’t give it to me!), “Ne le lui dis pas !” (Don’t tell him!).

On Saturday 19 April the flat in rue d’Austerlitz was full of people. There were still a few boxes in the corners, but nobody was looking at them.
Karim and Leïla had come with their daughter. Nathalie had brought champagne. Sophie had made a strawberry tart, the biggest of her life. Paul Martin was drawing everyone in his little notebook.
At eight o’clock the doorbell rang. It was Monsieur Garnier, with his aunt. Hélène was wearing the same elegant dress as the week before, and a little blue hat.
Madame Bernard was waiting by the piano. She had an envelope in her hands. Ioana saw that her hands were trembling, exactly like Hélène’s.
Ioana introduced them. The two women looked at each other for a long time without saying anything. Then Madame Bernard spoke first.
“Madame, I was Henri’s wife for fifty years. He wrote you this letter in 1963. He never sent it to you. I think that today he would want me to give it to you.”
Hélène took the envelope. She sat down on the sofa and read. Everyone fell silent. Even Karim’s daughter, who was six, understood that she had to be quiet.
When she had finished, Hélène looked up. “He was wounded… And all these years I thought he had forgotten me.”
“He never forgot you,” said Madame Bernard softly. “Every 3 May he whistled a waltz. All day long. I didn’t know why. Now I know.”
Hélène smiled through her tears. “3 May is my birthday.” She took Madame Bernard’s hand. “Thank you. You are more generous than I could ever have imagined.”
Then Julien sat down at the piano. He put the old score in front of him and played Henri’s waltz. This time it wasn’t a recording. It was Hélène’s real piano, in a real home, on a party night.
The two old ladies listened hand in hand. Victor climbed onto Hélène’s lap and fell asleep, as if he had always known her.
Later, on the balcony, Ioana asked Julien: “Do you think they’ll see each other again?”
Julien pointed to the living room. Hélène and Madame Bernard were looking at Madame Bernard’s old photos. They were laughing like two students.
“I think so,” said Julien. “And I promise you one thing: on 3 May we’ll have a party here. For the two of them. And I’ll play the waltz all evening.”
Ioana kissed him. Down in the street, the lights of Sophie’s bakery were going out one by one. Croix-Rousse was asleep. But in the first-floor flat, the music played on.

This is the letter Henri never sent, in 1963. Listen to the text twice, then read it aloud. At the end, answer 4 questions.
Marseille, 3 May 1963. My dear Hélène, today you are twenty-one. I have been thinking of you since this morning.
I came back from Algeria two months ago. I am alive, but my left hand doesn’t work properly any more. Two fingers no longer move.
The doctor says I will never play the piano again. I don’t believe it yet. But every morning I try, and every morning it’s worse.
Do you remember our promise? A house, a piano, your waltz every evening. I can’t play it for you any more.
So I won’t come back to Lyon. I’m going to leave on a ship. They say the sea heals everything. We’ll see.
Don’t wait for me, Hélène. You deserve a stronger man than me. You will be happy, I know it. You are the bravest person I know.
Keep the score. One day someone will play it for you better than I could.
And as for me, every 3 May, wherever I am, I will whistle your waltz. I promise you. Henri
